article_title: The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review.
citation: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/
title: WBA feedback should be specific and action-based to be effective for improving practice
description: The review concludes that for MSF to be a useful tool, the way it is used must be improved: "Comments should be provided and these should be specific and action-based." This principle holds that written feedback accompanying workplace based assessments should contain specific, actionable comments rather than global judgements or numerical scores alone, because global judgements do not indicate how trainees should behave to improve their practice.
requirements: Assessors must provide written comments rather than only numerical scores
Comments must be specific and action-based to inform a change in practice
constraints: Time constraints of a busy clinical workload, regarding WBA as cumbersome, lack of training on how to provide feedback, and lack of trust in the formative nature of assessment currently limit implementation
target_learning_goals: improving clinical performance through formative feedback
examples: The review reports that the greater space for free text in the TAB tool allows valuable information to be transmitted back to the trainee which they can use to inform a change in practice, rather than simply a numerical score
key_sources: Saedon H, Salleh S, Balakrishnan A, Imray CHE, Saedon M. (2012). The role of feedback in improving the effectiveness of workplace based assessments: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 12, 25. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3432628/

article_title: Higher Secondary Learners' Effectiveness towards Web Based Instruction (WBI) on Chemistry
citation: A. Sudha, S. Amutha. (2015). Higher Secondary Learners' Effectiveness towards Web Based Instruction (WBI) on Chemistry. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(7). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.030706
title: Web-based instruction module on purification of organic compounds with self-paced website exploration
description: The instructional element is a web-based instruction unit on the topic "Purification of organic compounds", covering nomenclature, formulas, functional groups, structures, characterization and reactions, delivered "using many related websites in chemistry, to acquire information". Students were given "opportunity ... to explore the websites at their own pace". Learning was measured with an investigator-prepared 25-question achievement test scored 0-20, analysed with SPSS 16.0.
requirements: Access to related chemistry websites for exploration
An achievement test to measure effectiveness
constraints: Studied only at higher secondary level in selected schools in Ariyalur district on a single organic chemistry topic
target_learning_goals: understanding organic chemistry concepts: nomenclature, formulas, functional groups, structures, characterization and reactions
examples: The experimental group explored chemistry websites at their own pace on purification of organic compounds, then took a 25-question achievement test scored 0-20.
key_sources: A. Sudha, S. Amutha. (2015). Higher Secondary Learners' Effectiveness towards Web Based Instruction (WBI) on Chemistry. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(7). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.030706

article_title: The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System
citation: Goksu, I. and Gulcu, A. (2016). The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Web Based Expert System (WBES) for RBT-based evaluation and reporting
description: WBES is a web-based expert system developed in this study that evaluates student tests according to the cognitive process dimension of RBT and generates reports pinpointing which levels a student lacks gains in. It has separate student, teacher and administrator interfaces, a question pool tagged with RBT levels and gains, test creation forms, and an expert module whose rules decide where additional training is needed. It was programmed in VB with Ajax, CSS, jQuery and Asp.net over an SQL Server database and "was published in the web environment under the domain name www.wtusogretim.com".
requirements: Teachers must have adequate information of RBT to upload questions and make reliable evaluations
constraints: The developed WBES system is only compatible with RBT
The expert system performs evaluations in accordance with some heuristic rules
target_learning_goals: algebraic expressions gains across the six RBT cognitive process levels
examples: Students in the experimental group solved the AST over the WBES system on the web, and the teacher used the WBES reports to direct each student to the supportive-education level he or she was lacking
key_sources: Goksu, I. and Gulcu, A. (2016). The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1117642

article_title: The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System
citation: Goksu, I. and Gulcu, A. (2016). The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Six-level supportive education routed by WBES diagnostic reports
description: In this pattern, students first take a diagnostic test through the expert system, which reports mastery per RBT cognitive process level; the teacher then runs supportive education organized into six levels matching the RBT processes. "Each student was taken to the one that he /she was lacking, which was determined in accordance with the reports provided by the WBES system." The sequence took two weeks and was delivered by the same teacher to both groups in the study.
requirements: A test instrument aligned to the RBT cognitive process dimension
A teacher informed about RBT to interpret the reports
constraints: Evaluated only in eighth-grade mathematics supportive-education courses over two weeks
target_learners: eighth-grade middle school students in weekend supportive education
target_learning_goals: closing diagnosed gaps in RBT cognitive process levels for algebraic expressions
examples: The experimental group's supportive education consisted of six stages over two weeks, with placement into levels determined by WBES reports
key_sources: Goksu, I. and Gulcu, A. (2016). The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1117642

article_title: A workplace-based learning program on clerkship of internal medicine improves medical student's clinical competence: a retrospective comparative study.
citation: Wang Ji-nuo, Lv Hanbing, Sun Yi, Cao Wen, Jiang Luhua. (2026). A workplace-based learning program on clerkship of internal medicine improves medical student's clinical competence: a retrospective comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08719-5
title: Workplace-based learning program (WBLP) integrating mini-CEX and DOPS with immediate feedback into an internal medicine clerkship
description: A workplace-based learning program layered onto a standard 9-week internal medicine clerkship across six subspecialty departments. It features "structured formative assessments every 1–2 weeks using mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercises (mini-CEX) and Direct Observation of Procedural Skills (DOPS), with immediate feedback provided after each assessment". Twelve senior attending supervisors delivered assessments after an 8-hour consensus training workshop covering rating forms, formative intent, and structured feedback models such as ask-tell-ask, with calibration via video-recorded encounters.
requirements: Trained supervisors: an 8-hour consensus training workshop on mini-CEX/DOPS rating forms, formative intent, and high-quality feedback principles
Regular assessment cadence (every 1–2 weeks) with immediate feedback after each assessment
constraints: Evaluated in a single-center retrospective cohort of fourth-year internal medicine clerks; the study was not designed to disentangle the effects of individual tools, feedback frequency, or supervisor characteristics
target_learners: Fourth-year undergraduate medical students on internal medicine clerkships
target_learning_goals: Clinical competence: medical knowledge, history taking, clinical reasoning, physical examination, procedural skills
examples: In the study, the WBLP group received mini-CEX and DOPS assessments every 1–2 weeks with immediate feedback, while controls received only standard theoretical and clinical skills training
key_sources: Wang Ji-nuo, Lv Hanbing, Sun Yi, Cao Wen, Jiang Luhua. (2026). A workplace-based learning program on clerkship of internal medicine improves medical student's clinical competence: a retrospective comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08719-5
